claim: A golden dataset is a carefully curated collection of test cases assembled by domain experts covering common patterns and tricky edge cases for a specific problem domain.
quote: a 'golden dataset' of test cases ... brainstorming the many different ways users might ask about dates, focusing on common patterns and tricky edge cases.

claim: A golden dataset is a high-quality, hand-labeled dataset serving as the 'ground truth' for LLM assessment, curated by subject matter experts.
quote: a high-quality, hand-labeled dataset that is used for training and evaluating the performance of these models ... the 'ground truth' ... often requiring the input of subject matter experts (SMEs)

claim: Without a shared golden reference set, model-quality debates stretch for weeks because teams argue feelings rather than facts.
quote: Model quality debates can stretch for weeks. Without shared references, teams argue feelings, not facts.

claim: Error analysis on real traces, not generic pre-built metrics, should decide what evals to write, grounding the golden dataset in failure modes unique to the application.
quote: Error analysis helps you decide what evals to write in the first place. It allows you to identify failure modes unique to your application and data.

claim: If an evaluation can't catch regressions or justify a launch in one slide, you're grading vibes; the fix is a golden set, a rubric, and statistics.
quote: if your evaluation can't catch regressions or justify a launch in one slide, you're grading vibes—and the fix is a golden set, a rubric, and some statistics.

claim: Synthetic test cases are bootstrapped by defining dimensions across three categories (Features, Scenarios, User Personas) and generating user inputs not outputs to avoid model bias.
quote: Think about three broad categories: Features (what capabilities does your AI need to support?), Scenarios (what situations will it encounter?), and User Personas (who will be using it and how?)

claim: Structured synthetic generation starts with ~20 hand-written tuples of dimensions, then scales in two LLM steps: generate structured tuples, then convert them to natural-language queries.
quote: Start by defining dimensions: categories that describe different aspects of user queries. Each dimension captures one type of variation in user behavior.

claim: EvalGen samples a random max of 16 responses from inputs for the human grading cycle, and developers benefit from being forced to grade a few responses before defining criteria.
quote: EvalGen takes a random sample of max 16 responses from your inputs, which limits the number of calls it needs to make per cycle.

claim: EvalGen asks humans to grade a subset of LLM outputs and uses that feedback to select assertion implementations (code or LLM-grader prompts) that better align with user grades.
quote: EvalGen asks humans to grade a subset of LLM outputs; this feedback is used to select implementations that better align with user grades.

claim: Synthetic eval test cases proved as effective as hand-crafted data for refining criteria and aligning with human preferences, with 83% of N=24 participants preferring synthetic generation over manual creation.
quote: generated synthetic data proved as effective as hand-crafted data for both refining evaluation criteria and aligning with user expectations.

claim: Vendor guidance treats golden datasets as living artifacts: start with a focused representative set covering core use cases and edge cases, then continuously pull validated production traces back in.
quote: Start with a focused set of representative inputs and carefully validated expected outputs, covering your core use cases and known edge cases.

claim: Braintrust converts production traces and reported failures into eval datasets and regression tests in one click, while LangSmith requires manual curation between tracing and evaluation.
quote: Braintrust can turn production traces into eval datasets with one click, building regression tests from real failures and edge cases, not synthetic examples.

claim: Standard chance-corrected inter-annotator agreement metrics are Cohen's Kappa, Fleiss' Kappa, and the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient, each suited to different annotation scenarios.
quote: Common statistical measures used to assess inter-annotator agreement include Cohen's Kappa, Fleiss' Kappa, and the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient, each suitable for different types of data and annotation scenarios.

claim: Cohen's kappa and Fleiss' kappa both correct for chance agreement; Cohen's handles two raters while Fleiss' generalizes to more than two, and reported kappa scores of 0.6-0.8 indicate substantial and above 0.8 almost-perfect agreement.
quote: Cohen's kappa designed for two raters while Fleiss' kappa generalizes the approach to settings with more than two raters ... strong agreement (0.6-0.8) to almost perfect agreement (> 0.8)

claim: LLM-as-judge exhibits self-preference bias rooted in perplexity: judges assign higher scores to lower-perplexity (more familiar) outputs than humans do, regardless of whether the model itself generated them.
quote: LLMs assign significantly higher evaluations to outputs with lower perplexity than human evaluators, regardless of whether the outputs were self-generated.

claim: LLM judges carry systematic biases including verbosity bias (preferring longer responses) and position bias (favoring the option presented first), and can align more with lay-user preferences than with subject-matter-expert standards.
quote: verbosity bias (where longer responses receive higher scores regardless of quality), and position bias (where responses presented earlier are preferred) ... LLM judgement is often more closely aligned with lay user preferences than SME standards

claim: A practical minimum golden dataset is 100 question-answer pairs, with 150 recommended for larger domains, to obtain statistically relevant numbers.
quote: a minimum dataset of 100 question-answer pairs is required, with 150 recommended for larger domains

claim: CLT-based confidence intervals dramatically underestimate uncertainty for LLM evals with fewer than a few hundred examples; Wilson intervals, clustered standard errors, and Bayesian methods are recommended instead.
quote: CLT approaches dramatically underestimate uncertainty in small-data scenarios ... advocates for ... Wilson intervals and clustered standard errors ... avoiding CLT-based statistics for benchmarks with fewer than a few hundred datapoints

claim: For 95% confidence with a 5% margin of error on an 80% metric, ~246 samples are needed; a 2.5% margin requires ~984; CI width scales as 1/sqrt(n).
quote: For 95% confidence with 5% margin of error on a metric expected to be 80%, approximately 246 samples are needed ... For 2.5% margin of error, 984 samples are required ... scales approximately with 1/sqrt(n)

claim: AntiLeakBench prevents contamination by automatically constructing samples with explicitly new knowledge absent from LLMs' training sets, enabling strictly contamination-free evaluation without human labor.
quote: construct[s] samples with explicitly new knowledge absent from LLMs' training sets ... a fully automated workflow to build and update our benchmark without human labor

claim: No semantic-preserving decontamination strategy achieves both high fidelity and high resistance; LLM-generated variants reach >0.95 resistance but drop fidelity to 0.66-0.75.
quote: No strategy lands in the top-right quadrant of the fidelity-resistance plane — high resistance and high fidelity ... LLM-generated variants—achieved high resistance (>0.95) but dropped fidelity to 0.66-0.75

claim: Golden dataset questions should reflect real customer queries, cover major expected domains, be self-contained, and avoid LLM-generated questions/answers without deep expert validation.
quote: Questions should, to the maximum extent possible, reflect what customers would ask in reality ... cover the major areas in the domains ... self-contained and assumes no other context ... an LLM answer as-is without proper, deep expert validation

claim: A 2025 study simulates training-data leakage in multiple-choice benchmarks to quantify how memorization of eval items inflates LLM accuracy and evades standard decontamination.
quote: Simulating Training Data Leakage in Multiple-Choice Benchmarks for LLM Evaluation

claim: Braintrust is the most complete single platform covering eval scoring, production tracing, A/B experiments, prompt playgrounds, CI/CD, datasets and annotation, with an AI agent (Loop) that auto-generates evaluation datasets and Brainstore for fast log storage.
quote: Braintrust is the most complete single platform in the space, covering eval scoring, production tracing, A/B experiments, prompt playgrounds, CI/CD integration, datasets, and annotation.

claim: A common production pattern pairs a lightweight CI/CD framework (DeepEval, RAGAS, or Promptfoo) with a platform for human annotation, regression tracking and dashboards (Braintrust, LangSmith, or Arize).
quote: using a lightweight framework for CI/CD gating (DeepEval, RAGAS, or Promptfoo) paired with a platform for human annotation, regression tracking, and stakeholder dashboards (Braintrust, LangSmith, or Arize)

claim: DeepEval includes tools for curating, versioning, and managing test datasets locally or on Confident AI, the most full-featured dataset lifecycle management among the open-source eval frameworks.
quote: DeepEval includes tools for curating, versioning, and managing test datasets for systematic evaluation (locally or on Confident AI)

claim: DeepEval is an open-source LLM evaluation framework that drops into pytest with 50+ scored metrics and pairs with the Confident AI platform for dataset management.
quote: DeepEval drops into pytest and gives you 50+ scored metrics with explanations

claim: Promptfoo is a CLI-first prompt-testing and red-teaming tool that runs locally and stores test cases as YAML configs in your repo, favoring config-as-code over a managed dataset store.
quote: Promptfoo is a CLI-first prompt testing and red-teaming tool that runs locally and uses YAML configs stored in your repo

claim: Ragas specializes in RAG evaluation and has built-in synthetic test-data generation that makes it easy to bootstrap an evaluation dataset, though it lacks broader dataset-management infrastructure.
quote: has built-in synthetic data generation makes it easy for teams to get started with RAG evaluation

claim: Inspect AI from the UK AI Security Institute is an open-source Python framework with opinionated primitives (dataset to Task to Solver to Scorer), multi-turn/agent workflows, sandboxed execution and a log viewer.
quote: Inspect AI is an open-source Python framework from the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) for building and running reproducible LLM evaluations. It ships opinionated primitives (dataset → Task → Solver → Scorer)

claim: Argilla is a collaborative human-in-the-loop annotation tool for building high-quality datasets, with bulk/focus labeling views, model suggestions with confidence scores, semantic-similarity ordering, response statuses, and distributed team progress tracking.
quote: model suggestions with confidence scores, metadata filtering, and customizable annotation guidelines to maintain consistent labeling standards

claim: Argilla's distilabel library can auto-label datasets with LLMs via the ArgillaLabeller class based on written guidelines, fields and questions, enabling LLM-assisted golden-set construction.
quote: The distilabel library can be used to label datasets with LLMs, utilizing the ArgillaLabeller class to label any dataset hosted on Argilla based on written dataset definitions, like guidelines, fields, and questions.

claim: Label Studio is widely-used open-source data labeling software that serves as a general-purpose annotation platform for building eval and training datasets.
quote: Label Studio is data labeling software

claim: OpenAI Evals is an open-source framework and registry of benchmarks for evaluating LLMs, providing a templated dataset/eval format that teams extend with custom golden sets.
quote: Evals is a framework for evaluating LLMs and LLM systems, and an open-source registry of benchmarks.

claim: Arize Phoenix is OpenTelemetry-native open-source observability best for production tracing, usable as a complementary tool to capture production traces that feed dataset curation rather than a complete eval/dataset solution.
quote: Phoenix is best for teams that prioritize production observability over comprehensive evaluation, and ideal as a complementary tool rather than a complete evaluation solution.

claim: Goodhart's law applies to LLM leaderboards: once labs treat a ranking as the target the metric loses validity, and selective disclosure gamed Arena scores — a modest increase in access to Arena data could boost a model's performance by up to 112%.
quote: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure... even a modest increase in access to Arena data could boost a model's Arena performance by up to 112%

claim: A common anti-pattern is treating custom evaluation as a one-time task with static offline datasets that quickly become outdated; dataset drift requires the eval set to shift as user behavior evolves.
quote: custom evaluation as a one-time task, relying on static offline datasets that quickly become outdated... Dataset Drift... your evaluation dataset must accompany this shift
